blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Deciding on the hypothesis from the evidence, evaluating the reliability of the methods, and extending the enquiry to a new question.

blocks.heading: The conclusion
blocks.text: A conclusion states whether the hypothesis is true, false or partly true, and then supports the decision with paired figures from the data. The decision first: true, false, partly true, the three words a conclusion opens with. The evidence next, in pairs: the values at two sites or two dates that show the pattern, 12.4 centimetres at site 1 against 4.8 at site 4, so the bedload does shrink downstream. A decision without figures is an opinion, and a conclusion that states no decision loses the mark the decision carries, so both halves are written, judgement then proof.

blocks.heading: True without proof
blocks.text: A conclusion that says the hypothesis is true and stops has answered nothing, because nothing in it shows why. The reader needs a figure that proves the decision: the sites, the values and the direction they run. The test is whether there is a figure in the conclusion that could not have been written by someone who never saw the data.

blocks.heading: The evaluation
blocks.text: Reliability means the method would give the same results if repeated, and the evaluation asks it of every choice. The sample: ten pebbles is a sample the sea laughs at, and fifty widens it. The sites: two sites cannot show a pattern a valley long, and eight can. The timing: a weekday survey says nothing about Saturday, and a dry-season river says nothing about the flood. The method: a float catches the surface, a flow meter reads the channel, and the error of the instrument is named. Each evaluation names what to change and why the change makes the results more reliable, more sites, a larger sample, a different time, a method less open to error, because an evaluation is a repair list, not a confession.

blocks.heading: "Repeat it" is not an improvement
blocks.text: Suggesting "repeat it" or "do it again" as the improvement changes nothing, so the same errors return with the same results. The improvement names what is done differently and what defect it fixes: repeat the count at four more sites, because two sites cannot show a fall with distance; sample fifty pebbles instead of ten, because a small sample swings on one boulder. What exactly is done differently, and what does it fix, is the pair an improvement carries.

blocks.heading: The extension
blocks.text: An extension tests something new: another place, the same enquiry on a second river to see whether the finding holds; another season, the pedestrian count repeated in December against March; another variable, the pebble survey that adds shape to size, or the quality survey that adds interviews to scores. The new enquiry answers a different question, which is what separates an extension from a rerun, and a good extension follows from the first enquiry's own findings, the pattern that surprised, the site that broke the trend, the variable that went unmeasured.

blocks.heading: An enquiry closed, start to finish
blocks.text: Close the river study as the discipline runs. The hypothesis: bedload becomes smaller and rounder downstream, measurable, directed, testable. The data: twenty stones a site, every fifth stone along a tape, callipers and a roundness scale, four sites on one day. The description: the means fall from 14.2 to 5.1 centimetres and the roundness rises from 2.1 to 3.2, smooth trends, no exceptions. The conclusions: both hypotheses true, each decision followed by its paired figures. The evaluation: fifty stones a site would steady the means, six sites would fill the gaps, two judges would dilute the roundness judgement. The extension: a second catchment, because the finding's reach is a different question from the finding itself. One enquiry, and every stage is a skill this topic has taught.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The conclusion discipline, decision then paired figures, is the levels-marked case-study answer of Paper 1 in miniature, and the evaluation skills are what the practical tasks of this topic rehearse end to end.

blocks.heading: An evaluation worked on one enquiry
blocks.text: An evaluation worked on the resort survey above. The sample: 60 interviews at one site is a small sample for a town that holds thousands, so the improvement is 120 interviews across two sites, and what it fixes is the sample's reach, because one promenade cannot speak for the shoppers. The timing: a single Saturday says nothing about Tuesday, so the improvement is a weekday repeat, and what it fixes is the day's bias, because the market-day crowd is a different population. The question wording: the pilot caught two faults, so the improvement is a second pilot when the questions change again, and what it fixes is the wording faults a changed form reintroduces. Each improvement names what is done differently and what defect it removes, which is the discipline the evaluation marks reward.

blocks.heading: A conclusion and an extension, worked
blocks.text: A conclusion and an extension, worked on the same survey. The hypothesis, that visitors to the resort are mostly day-trippers from within 50 kilometres, found 41 of 60 interviews under 50 kilometres, so 41 / 60 x 100 = 68 per cent, and the conclusion is true, stated with its paired figures, 68 per cent within 50 kilometres against 32 per cent beyond. The extension follows from what the enquiry did not ask: where the 32 per cent came from and why they came so far, so the extension is a second questionnaire at the overnight accommodation, comparing the stayers' distances and reasons with the day-trippers', which answers a different question rather than repeating the first. Paper 4 examines the coursework criteria through fieldwork scenarios, and the syllabus sets its marks in the same proportions as the enquiry itself, knowledge with understanding, collecting data, presenting data, analysis, and conclusion and evaluation, twelve marks each.
